holding: Consequently, the instant civil revision is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree dated 16.02.2019 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Gujrat, are hereby set aside, and the consolidated judgment and decree dated 07.03.2016 passed by the learned Civil Judge, Gujrat, are restored. Resultantly, the petitioners' suit for declaration, cancellation of the disputed mutations and permanent injunction stands decreed in terms of the judgment of the learned Trial Court, while the suit instituted by respondent No.6 for possession through partition stands dismissed. (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) Judge APPROVED FOR REPORTING Judge *A.H.S.*

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 03.11.2026. Petitioners by: M/s. Aitzaz Ahsan and Ch. Shaukat Ali Javaid, Advocates. Respondents by: M/s. Muhammad Saad Bin Ghazi, Assistant Advocate General and Muhammad Zain Qazi, Assistant Attorney General. M/s. Mian Mushtaq Mehdi Akhtar and Muhammad Ashfaq Malik, Advocates (for respondent No.6). Remaining respondents ex parte. MUHAMMAD SAJID MEHMOOD SETHI, J.- Through instant revision petition, the petitioners, being legal heirs of Muhammad Inayat (deceased), have called in question the judgment and decree dated 16.02.2019 passed by learned Additional District Judge, Gujrat, whereby the consolidated judgment and decree dated 07.03.2016 passed by learned Civil Judge, Gujrat, was reversed. Consequently, petitioners' suit for declaration, cancellation of documents and permanent injunction was dismissed as barred by limitation, whereas suit instituted by respondent No.6 for possession through partition was decreed by way of a preliminary decree. I. FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Briefly, the controversy relates to one kanal of land situated in Mauza Jaliani, Tehsil and District Gujrat, abutting the main G.T. Road, forming part of Khewat No.314, Khatoni No.556, Square No.29, Khasra Nos.6/1 and 6/2 (hereinafter referred to as the "suit land"). The said property originally belonged to Muhammad Inayat, predecessor- in-interest of the petitioners. The petitioners instituted a suit on 13.08.2011, asserting that after the death of Muhammad Inayat on 28.06.2010, they approached the revenue authorities for attestation of his inheritance mutation and, during those proceedings in August 2010, discovered that one kanal of the suit land had already been transferred in favour of respondent No.6, Nadeem Ahmad Sindhu, through Mutation No.2493 dated 15.04.2005, Mauza Jaliani. The said mutation was allegedly founded upon an exchange of one kanal of land situated in Mauza Sahinwal Khurd, reflected through connected Mutation No.722 dated 15.12.2004. The petitioners challenged both mutations as fraudulent, forged, unexecuted and without lawful authority, maintaining that their predecessor had never consented to the alleged exchange. Respondent No.6 contested the suit, claiming that a valid oral exchange had taken place between him and Muhammad Inayat, whereby the suit land was exchanged for one kanal of land situated in Mauza Sahinwal Khurd. He further asserted that an additional amount of Rs.700,000/- had been paid to Muhammad Inayat to equalise the difference in value of the two properties. On the strength of the alleged exchange, respondent No.6 also instituted a suit for possession through partition, claiming himself to be a co-sharer in the suit land. Both suits were consolidated and, after recording evidence, the learned Civil Judge, Gujrat, through judgment and decree dated 07.03.2016, decreed the petitioners' suit and dismissed the partition suit of respondent No.6. However, the learned Additional District Judge, Gujrat, through the impugned judgment dated 16.02.2019, reversed the findings of the learned Trial Court, dismissed the petitioners' suit as time-barred under Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and granted a preliminary decree for partition in favour of respondent No.6. Hence, this revision petition. II. CONTENTIONS OF THE PARTIES

Learned counsel for the petitioners contends that the learned appellate Court failed to appreciate that mutations are merely revenue entries and do not, by themselves, confer title. He adds that in terms of Sections 54 and 118 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the alleged exchange required a legally recognised mode of transfer, whereas no registered exchange instrument was produced. He further argues that respondent No.6 failed to produce any independent witness to establish the alleged oral transaction or to prove the execution and consent of Muhammad Inayat. He maintains that the alleged payment of Rs.700,000/- was also not substantiated, despite the categorical admissions of the revenue officials that no such payment was recorded in the Roznamcha Waqiati or the relevant mutation proceedings. He further points out that the land at Mauza Jaliani was situated along the main G.T. Road and possessed an urban and commercial character, whereas the reciprocal land at Mauza Sahinwal Khurd was allegedly sandy, barren and situated towards the river side, with no other property of Muhammad Inayat situated in that Mauza; according to learned counsel, this marked disparity in the nature, location and value of the properties, coupled with the failure to prove the alleged balancing payment, further undermined the genuineness of the purported exchange. He further maintains that the petitioners acquired knowledge of the disputed mutations in August 2010 and instituted the suit within time, while the learned Appellate Court erroneously drew an adverse inference from their appearance through a special attorney and relied upon an unsafe comparison of disputed signatures and thumb impressions. In support of his submissions, he referred to Haji Abdullah Khan and others v. Nisar Muhammad Khan and others (PLD 1965 Supreme Court 690), Hakim Khan v. Nazeer Ahmad Lughmani and 10 others (1992 SCMR 1832), Muhammad Younus Khan and 12 others v. Government of N.-W.F.P. through Secretary, Forest and Agriculture, Peshawar and others (1993 SCMR 618), Almas Ahmad Fiaz v. Secretary Government of the Punjab Housing and Physical Planning Development, Lahore and another (2006 SCMR 783), Evacuee Trust Property Board and others v. Mst. Sakina Bibi and others (2007 SCMR 262), Nabi Bakhsh v. Fazal Hussain (2008 SCMR 1454), Irshad Khan v. The State (2026 SCMR 87), Anayat Ali Shah v. Anwar Hussain and 2 others (1995 MLD 1714) and Bashir Ahmad Khan and others v. Ghulam Sadar-ud-Din Khan and others (2012 CLC 699).

Conversely, learned counsel for respondent No.6, duly assisted by the learned Law Officer, maintains that the entries in the Register Haqdaran Zamin (Ex.D-8) carry a presumption of correctness under the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, read with Article 129(e) of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. He argues that disparity in the values of the exchanged properties and non-delivery of physical possession do not, by themselves, invalidate an exchange, particularly as the question of disparity was not specifically pleaded in the plaint. In support of his submissions, he has placed reliance upon Elahi Bakhsh through Legal Heirs and others v. Muhammad Iqbal and another (2014 SCMR 1217), Muhammad Irshad and 4 others v. Sardar Khan (1981 CLC 124), Ghulam Hussain v. Jam Allah Dad through Legal Heirs (PLD 1989 Lahore 73) and Raja Muhammad Saeed Khan v. Haji Nazir Ahmed and 11 others (PLD 2007 Supreme Court (AJ&K) 63). He further contends that the petitioners failed to appear personally as witnesses and that Muhammad Inayat remained alive for more than five years after sanction of the mutations without challenging them. In support of his objection of limitation, he has referred to Abdul Haq and another v. Mst. Surrya Begum and others (2002 SCMR 1330), Faqir Muhammad and 8 others v. Abdul Momin and 2 others (PLD 2003 Supreme Court 594), Muhammad Rustam and another v. Mst. Makhan Jan and others (2013 SCMR 299) and Jam Muhammad Ismail and others v. Jam Bahawal and others (2012 MLD 1545). Reliance has further been placed upon Qadir Bakhsh and 10 others v. Kh. Nizam-ud-Din Khan and 4 others (1997 SCMR 1267), Mst. Hamida Begum v. Muhammad Saleem (1988 CLC 2456), Muhammad Rafique v. Muhammad (1989 CL C 1318), Pir Bakhsh v. Rahim Bakhsh and others (PLD 1992 Lahore 385), Muhammad Luqman v. Bashir Ahmad (PLD 1994 Karachi 492), Noor Muhammad v. Jamal Din and others (2000 CLC 305), Messrs Society Oil Dealers, Karachi v. District Judge, Karachi and another (2003 MLD 205), Zafar Yasin and 2 others v. Abdur Rashid Khan through Legal Heirs and 5 others (2003 YLR 2478), Mst. Mohsina Saeed Tauni v. Muhammad Asif and others (PLD 2005 Karachi 585), Messrs Kashmirian Pvt. Ltd. through Shomaila Loan Marker and 6 others v. Ghulam Nabi Gujjar and another (2006 CLC 482), Fateh Muhammad through L.Rs. and others v. Fida Hussain Shah through L.Rs. (2007 CLC 1885), Syed Iftikhar Hussain v. Shaikh Abdul Aziz and another (2007 YLR 2116), Muhammad Saleem v. Muhammad Tariq (2009 CLC 1295), Muhammad Ashraf v. Ghulam Hussain and 4 others (2010 CLC 841), Syed Azhar Hussain v. Muhammad Aslam and 8 others (2010 MLD 1162) and Khuda Bakhsh Javed and 4 others v. Ahmad and 6 others (2013 YLR 2576).
I have heard the learned counsel for the parties and examined the available record with their assistance. III. SCOPE OF REVISIONAL JURISDICTION

The learned Courts below have returned conflicting findings on the validity of the alleged exchange, the burden of proof, the evidentiary value of the disputed mutations and limitation. The controversy involves the legal efficacy of an alleged exchange of immovable property and the burden of proving the underlying transaction. The impugned judgment therefore requires examination, not for reappraisal of evidence, but to ascertain whether the learned Appellate Court applied the correct legal principles and properly considered the material evidence. Such examination falls within the limits of revisional jurisdiction.

Learned counsel for respondent No.6 objected to the petitioners raising the requirement of a registered instrument under Sections 118 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 for the first time in revision. The objection is misconceived. Respondent No.6 himself asserts that the alleged exchange was oral and was given effect through Mutation Nos.722 dated 15.12.2004 and 2493 dated 15.04.2005, without any registered exchange deed. The nature of the transaction being evident from the pleadings and evidence, its legal efficacy under the applicable statutory provisions is a question of law which this Court may examine in revisional jurisdiction. The principle is supported by Haji Abdullah Khan and Mst. Sakina Bibi supra. IV. POINTS FOR DETERMINATION

The following points arise for determination: A. Whether the alleged exchange was legally established and satisfied the requirements of Sections 54 and 118 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; B. Whether respondent No.6 discharged the burden of proving the alleged exchange, consent of Muhammad Inayat, execution and payment of Rs.700,000/-; C. Whether the learned Appellate Court correctly appreciated the evidence concerning the petitioners' appearance through a special attorney and on the comparison of disputed signatures/thumb impressions; D. Whether the petitioners' suit was barred by limitation; and E. Whether the preliminary decree for partition could legally be sustained. V. DISCUSSION AND FINDINGS A. LEGAL EFFICACY OF THE ALLEGED EXCHANGE AND EVIDENTIARY VALUE OF MUTATIONS

The principal controversy is whether Muhammad Inayat had validly exchanged the suit land with respondent No.6 and, consequently, whether the latter acquired a lawful title thereto. Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 provides that an exchange of property is completed in the manner prescribed for the transfer of property by sale. Under Section 54 of the said Act, a sale of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards can be made only by a registered instrument. Thus, where the statutory requirement of registration applies to the properties in question, an alleged oral exchange, merely followed by revenue mutations, cannot by itself be treated as a legally completed transfer of ownership.

A mutation is a revenue entry that records a transaction; it does not create one. It is declaratory of an earlier act, not constitution of title, and it can rise no higher than the transaction it records. In Hakim Khan supra, Mst. Ramzanu Bibi v. Ibrahim (deceased) through L.Rs. and others (2025 SCMR 955) and Zaffar Afzal and others v. Ashiq Hussain (PLD 2023 SC 456), the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that a mutation does not, by itself, create title and that the person deriving title thereunder must prove that the transferor had parted with ownership in favour of the transferee. The burden of proving the transaction embodied in the mutation rests upon the person claiming title through it. The same principle was reiterated in Muhammad Ishfaq and another v. Salma Begum (2026 SCMR 1523) and Bashir Ahmad Khan supra, wherein it was observed that a mutation is not, by itself, a document of title and that its beneficiary must establish the transaction and valid attestation through independent and cogent evidence.

The recent judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Abdullah and others v. Waryam and others (PLJ 2026 SC 287), further clarifies that revenue authorities exercise limited jurisdiction concerning the correction and maintenance of revenue records; their decisions are administrative and tentative in nature and do not conclusively determine ownership or adjudicate allegations of fraud and misrepresentation. Such controversies fall within the jurisdiction of the Civil Court under Section 9, C.P.C. Consequently, Mutation Nos.722 dated 15.12.2004 and 2493 dated 15.04.2005, and the subsequent revenue entries, could not by themselves conclusively establish respondent No.6’s ownership. Their legal effect had to be determined by examining the transaction upon which they were founded. It is, however, equally important to clarify that mere non-compliance with a procedural requirement by revenue officials does not, in every case, automatically invalidate an otherwise established transaction. In Hakim Khan supra, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that although the requirements of Section 42 of the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967 are mandatory directions to revenue officials, their non- compliance does not, by itself, render the underlying transaction invalid. The decisive question remains whether the transaction through which title is claimed has been duly established. Likewise, Muhammad Younus Khan supra, by majority, reiterates that an allegation of fraud must be specifically pleaded and established through reliable evidence; it does not, however, elevate a mutation into an independent instrument of title.

There is yet another legal infirmity in the manner in which the documentary evidence was brought on record. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Rustam and others v. Jehangir (deceased) through LRs. (2023 SCMR 730) has held that documents produced through the statement of learned counsel, without being tendered in evidence by the party concerned and subjected to the requisite process of proof, cannot be taken into consideration. In the instant case, the entire documentary evidence has been placed on record admittedly through the statement of learned counsel for the respondent No.6, which could not be read into evidence. The same principle was reiterated in Manzoor Hussain (deceased) through L.Rs. v. Misri Khan (PLD 2020 Supreme Court 749), Mst. Akhtar Sultana v. Major Retd. Muzaffar Khan Malik through his legal heirs and others (PLD 2021 Supreme Court 715), Mst. Rasoolan Bibi v. Province of Punjab and others (2023 CLC 1171) and National Highway Authority, Islamabad through Project Director Zafar Mehmood v. Muhammad Afzal Bhatti and another (2024 CLC 1246). B. BURDEN OF PROOF AND EVIDENCE REGARDING THE ALLEGED EXCHANGE

Under Articles 117 and 118 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, the burden lies on the party who asserts a fact and who would fail if no evidence was led. In the present case, respondent No.6 is the beneficiary of the alleged exchange and claims ownership of the suit land through the two mutations in question. Therefore, the initial burden rested upon him to establish that Muhammad Inayat had in fact agreed to exchange the suit land with him, that the transaction was entered into with his free consent and that it was legally completed in accordance with the applicable law. The petitioners, on the other hand, were required to establish their pleaded case, including any specific allegation of fraud or misrepresentation. These are distinct evidentiary burdens and should not be conflated. In Nabi Bakhsh supra, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, while dealing with a disputed exchange of immovable property, held that where the plaintiff denies having exchanged his property with the defendant, the onus lies heavily upon the defendant to establish that a valid exchange had taken place and that the mutation was attested with the consent and at the instance of the plaintiff. The same approach was adopted by this Court in Anayat Ali Shah supra, where the Court examined the genuineness and voluntary execution of the disputed exchange in the light of the surrounding circumstances, including the continued possession of the person challenging it.

Respondent No.6, while appearing as DW-1, made certain significant admissions during cross-examination concerning the comparative location and value of the properties allegedly exchanged. He admitted that the suit property situated at Mauza Jaliani was abutting the main G.T. Road and had already been commercialised when he constructed his factory there in 1995. When confronted with the suggestion that there was a huge difference between the prices of the properties situated at Mauza Jaliani and Mauza Sahinwal Khurd, he acknowledged that it was for this very reason that he had paid Rs.700,000/- to Muhammad Inayat. Significantly, however, he expressed ignorance about the prevailing per-marla rates of the properties in the two Mauzas. This admission assumes importance because the alleged payment was specifically projected as an adjustment for the substantial difference in the values of the exchanged properties, yet respondent No.6 could not furnish any particulars regarding their comparative valuation or the basis on which the said amount was determined. Furthermore, DW-3 Waqar Hussain Khan, Ex-Tehsildar, Gujrat, admitted that, for the purpose of an exchange mutation, the properties should be of the same nature and classification and their market values should also be equal. Similarly, DW-4 Muhammad Afzal, Patwari, acknowledged that the properties situated in both Mauzas should be of equal value for the purpose of an exchange mutation. Although DW-3 stated that neither party had raised any objection before him regarding payment or receipt of the amount at the time of attestation of the impugned mutations, DW-4 categorically stated that the parties had not disclosed to him, in his presence, any payment or receipt of money in connection with the disputed mutations. Thus, the statements of the revenue officials do not furnish any independent corroboration of the alleged payment of Rs.700,000/-. Rather, the absence of any contemporaneous disclosure or corresponding entry in the relevant revenue proceedings assumes significance when considered alongside the admission of respondent No.6 himself.

The nature of the property situated at Mauza Sahinwal Khurd also requires consideration in this context. DW-5 Khalid Pervaiz, Patwari, admitted during cross-examination that, according to the Record of Rights for the year 2008–09 (Ex.D-6), all the 35 Qita'at of the relevant Khasra numbers relating to Mauza Sahinwal Khurd were recorded as Ghair Mumkin/Sandi. Although the said entry pertains to a subsequent period and, therefore, cannot by itself conclusively establish the precise classification or market value of the property at the time of the alleged exchange in 2004–05, it is nevertheless a relevant circumstance requiring consideration alongside the location and commercial character of the suit property situated on the main G.T. Road, Mauza Jaliani. The cumulative effect of these circumstances assumes particular significance because respondent No.6 himself attributed the payment of Rs.700,000/- to the difference in the values of the two properties, yet neither produced any valuation assessment nor furnished any reliable particulars regarding the prevailing rates in the respective Mauzas. It is clarified that disparity in the values of exchanged properties does not, by itself, render an exchange invalid, nor does the law invariably require that the properties exchanged must be of identical market value. Nevertheless, where a substantial difference in value is admitted by the beneficiary of the transaction and a specific payment is asserted to explain that difference, the genuineness and actual payment of such amount become relevant circumstances in determining whether the alleged exchange was genuinely agreed upon and acted upon by the parties. The absence of corroborative evidence in this regard cannot, therefore, be brushed aside as immaterial.

The authorities relied upon by respondent No.6, including Elahi Bakhsh through Legal Heirs and others v. Muhammad Iqbal and another (2014 SCMR 1217), may support the proposition that mere disparity in the values of exchanged properties does not invalidate an exchange. However, such proposition does not dispense with the obligation of the beneficiary to establish the underlying transaction, its voluntary execution and the consent of the transferor. In the present case, the admitted commercial character and roadside location of the Jaliani property, the acknowledged difference in the values of the two properties, the asserted adjustment of Rs.700,000/-, the absence of reliable particulars concerning the comparative valuation and the lack of independent corroboration of the alleged payment were material circumstances requiring cumulative appreciation. These circumstances, when examined alongside the remaining evidence concerning the alleged execution and attestation of the mutations, could not be ignored merely because the revenue entries had been incorporated in the official record. As regards the objection raised by learned counsel for respondent No.6 that the disparity in the values of the exchanged properties was not specifically pleaded in the plaint, it is sufficient to observe that the disparity was admitted by the defence witnesses themselves, who also failed to establish the alleged payment of Rs.700,000/-. In these circumstances, the objection is misconceived.

The question of disputed signatures and thumb impressions also required careful examination. Article 84 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 empowers the Court to compare disputed handwriting or signatures with admitted or proved specimens. An expert opinion is not invariably indispensable; nevertheless, comparison must be undertaken cautiously and only with duly established standards. The Court must also distinguish between the examination of handwriting or signatures and the identification of thumb impressions, which may require separate evidentiary consideration.

Accordingly, the mere absence of an expert report would not, by itself, render the disputed mutations inadmissible or invalid. Conversely, a conclusion regarding execution cannot safely rest upon an unsubstantiated comparison or upon specimens whose authenticity has not been established. The learned Appellate Court was required to examine the original revenue record, the evidence concerning the alleged execution and the circumstances in which the disputed signatures or thumb impressions were obtained, before treating the transaction as proved.

The requirements of Section 42 of the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, including the prescribed inquiry and identification, are intended to ensure that revenue entries are made after proper verification. Their significance in the present case was required to be assessed in the light of Hakim Khan supra. The judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Irshad Khan supra, although arising from criminal proceedings under a special enactment, reiterates the general principle that where the law prescribes a particular procedure, the same must be followed. That principle may be noticed in the present context, but the criminal standard of proof or the consequences of procedural lapses in that case cannot be transplanted wholesale into the present civil dispute. C. APPEARANCE THROUGH SPECIAL ATTORNEY AND ADVERSE INFERENCE

The petitioners’ failure to appear personally could not, by itself, be treated as proof that the alleged exchange had taken place. Order III, Rules 1 and 2, C.P.C. permit a recognised agent or attorney to act on behalf of a party; however, the evidentiary value of an attorney’s testimony is confined to matters within his personal knowledge or acts performed by him. Equally, an attorney cannot be expected to prove a transaction allegedly entered into by a deceased predecessor unless he possesses personal knowledge of the relevant circumstances. Reliance is placed upon Mrs. Zakia Hussain and another v. Syed Farooq Hussain (PLD 2020 Supreme Court 401) Once on 13.10.2016, this Court during the course of hearing had noted that the respondent, during the course of trial, had not appeared as his witness and his attorney, who was not fully conversant with the facts and circumstances of the case personally, had deposed in the Court which is nothing less than a hearsay and the attorney does not fall within the purview of Order III Rules 1 and 2 of Civil Procedure Code 1908 (C.P.C.).

Muhammad Inayat had died on 28.06.2010, whereas the suit was instituted on 13.08.2011. The petitioners’ non-appearance could not relieve respondent No.6 of the burden to prove the transaction allegedly entered into with Muhammad Inayat during his lifetime. An adverse inference, if otherwise warranted by the circumstances, could not substitute for proof of the very transaction through which respondent No.6 claimed ownership. D. LIMITATION

The question of limitation is undoubtedly required to be examined by the Court irrespective of whether it has been raised by the opposite party, as mandated by Section 3 of the Limitation Act, 1908. This principle was reiterated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Almas Ahmad Fiaz (supra). However, the obligation to examine limitation necessarily entails determination of the correct statutory provision, the point at which the right to sue accrued and the effect of any pleaded concealment or fraud. The mere fact that a mutation was entered in the revenue record does not, without more, answer those questions.

In Bashir Ahmad Khan supra, this Court held that mutation proceedings are not judicial proceedings and do not, by themselves, provide the starting point of limitation. It further observed that, in a declaratory suit concerning a wrongful mutation, limitation is to be examined with reference to the threat to the plaintiff’s title; where the plaintiffs remain co-sharers, the continuing nature of their rights and the subsequent revenue entries may also be material. The said judgment relied upon Moolchand and 9 others v. Muhammad Yousaf (Udhamdas) and 3 others (PLD 1994 Supreme Court 462), Haji through his Legal Heirs and others v. Khuda Yar through his Legal Heirs (PLD 1987 Supreme Court 453) and Muhammad Yaqoob v. Mst. Sardaran Bibi and others (PLD 2020 Supreme Court 338). These principles required consideration by the learned Appellate Court, particularly if the petitioners continued to assert their inherited rights and possession in the suit Khata.

The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mst. Fatima Bibi through L.Rs. and another v. Altaf Ahmed and others (2009 SCMR 693), Baja through L.Rs. and others v. Mst. Bakhan and others (2015 SCMR 1704), also emphasised the relevance of the date on which the affected party acquired knowledge of the alleged fraudulent transaction. Although Mst. Fatima Bibi concerned a decree challenged on the ground of fraud and referred to Article 95 of the Limitation Act, 1908, that provision cannot automatically be applied to the present proceedings. The applicable article has to be identified in the light of the substance of the relief sought, while the plea of concealment, if properly pleaded and established, must also be examined in the context of Section 18 of the Act.

The petitioners’ case is that they acquired knowledge of the impugned mutations in August 2010 during proceedings for inheritance mutation following the death of Muhammad Inayat, and thereafter instituted the suit on 13.08.2011. The fact that Muhammad Inayat remained alive for several years after the impugned mutations does not, by itself, establish that he had knowledge of the alleged exchange or had acquiesced in it. Likewise, the mere existence of entries in the revenue record cannot automatically be equated with actual knowledge of the petitioners. The learned Appellate Court was required to examine the pleadings and evidence regarding the date of knowledge, the nature of the petitioners’ rights in the Khata, their possession, and the date on which their title was first threatened or denied.

In the present case, the petitioners instituted the suit on 13.08.2011, within approximately one year of acquiring knowledge of the disputed mutations in August 2010, as asserted in their plaint. The mere fact that Muhammad Inayat remained alive for approximately five years after sanction of the impugned mutations does not, in the absence of evidence establishing his actual knowledge of the alleged exchange or an earlier denial of his proprietary rights, furnish a lawful basis for computing limitation against the petitioners from the dates of those mutations. Furthermore, the record does not establish that respondent No.6 had taken possession of the suit land pursuant to the disputed exchange so as to constitute an earlier actual denial of the proprietary rights of Muhammad Inayat. In these circumstances, and having regard to the nature of the relief claimed, the suit, being essentially declaratory in character, was governed by Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908, under which the period of six years commenced when the petitioners' right to sue accrued upon discovery of the disputed transaction and the consequential threat to their inherited rights. The suit having been instituted within one year of such discovery was, therefore, clearly within the prescribed period of limitation. The requirements of Section 18 of the Act, concerning concealment of the right to sue through fraud, consequently do not require invocation for sustaining the institution of the suit within time. The learned Appellate Court, therefore, erred in dismissing the petitioners' suit as time-barred merely with reference to the dates of sanction of the impugned mutations, without determining the actual accrual of the right to sue in accordance with the applicable law. E. CONSEQUENTIAL EFFECT ON THE PARTITION PROCEEDINGS

The claim of respondent No.6 for partition and possession was founded upon his assertion that he had acquired ownership of the suit land through the alleged exchange. His entitlement to seek partition was, therefore, dependent upon proof of the title and co-sharer status claimed by him. If the underlying exchange is not established, or if it is found incapable of transferring title in the manner required by Sections 118 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the consequential mutations cannot independently confer upon him the status of a co- sharer. In that eventuality, the foundation of his partition claim would cease to exist.

The principle that a subsequent transaction or consequential entry cannot survive independently where its foundational transaction is not established is also reflected in Baja through L.Rs. and others v. Mst. Bakhan and others (2015 SCMR 1704). Nevertheless, the petitioners must succeed on the strength of their own established rights, and not merely on the weakness of respondent No.6’s case. The learned Appellate Court was, therefore, required to determine both the petitioners’ title and the validity of the transaction relied upon by respondent No.6, before reversing the decree of the learned Trial Court and granting a preliminary decree for partition. VI. CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, the material questions concerning the legal mode of transfer under Sections 118 and 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the burden of proving the alleged exchange, the evidentiary value of the mutations, the disputed execution and the petitioners’ asserted date of knowledge required independent determination. The impugned judgment could not properly rest merely upon the existence of the revenue entries, the petitioners’ non- appearance in person or the fact that Muhammad Inayat remained alive after the mutations. The learned Appellate Court was required to examine whether respondent No.6 had established the underlying exchange through legally admissible and reliable evidence and whether the petitioners’ suit was barred under the correct provision of the Limitation Act, 1908. Failure to address these material aspects, if borne out by the record, constitutes a material misapplication of law and misreading or non-reading of evidence warranting interference under Section 115, C.P.C.

Consequently, the instant civil revision is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree dated 16.02.2019 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Gujrat, are hereby set aside, and the consolidated judgment and decree dated 07.03.2016 passed by the learned Civil Judge, Gujrat, are restored. Resultantly, the petitioners' suit for declaration, cancellation of the disputed mutations and permanent injunction stands decreed in terms of the judgment of the learned Trial Court, while the suit instituted by respondent No.6 for possession through partition stands dismissed. (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) Judge APPROVED FOR REPORTING Judge *A.H.S.*
